explanation: Depth-first search keeps a current path. Enter only white in-bounds cells, mark each visited cell black, and recursively try four neighbors. Pop a cell from the path when all continuations fail; retain the path on success.
timeComplexity: O(RC): each cell is marked at most once and considers four neighbors. Every reached cell has at most four neighbors and is recorded or marked once; the worst-case frontier/path visits the whole maze.
spaceComplexity: O(RC) worst-case recursive stack and path; C++ additionally copies the input maze. Predecessors/frontier or visited markings/path can involve every maze cell; C++ also stores a maze copy.
attribution: Unmodified EPIJudge reference source: epi_judge_java_solutions/epi/SearchMaze.java. Original contributors; repository LICENSE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).
correctness: The path is always a sequence of orthogonally adjacent original white cells from the start. Marking on entry prevents cycles and repeated exploration. Failed branches cannot reach the destination, so discarding them is safe; a successful branch leaves an endpoint-inclusive valid path. Exhausting reachable cells proves no path exists.
walkthrough: In [[0,0,1],[1,0,0],[0,0,0]], the path must start (0,0)→(0,1)→(1,1). C++/Java then try (1,2)→(2,2); Python tries (2,1)→(2,0), backtracks, then reaches (2,2). Both are valid; no shortest-path guarantee is required. JSON arguments are [maze,[startRow,startColumn],[endRow,endColumn]]. Observed true means a valid path was accepted; observed false for distinct unreachable endpoints corresponds to an empty returned path. The wrapper also observes true for any empty result when start=end, a weaker check than the callable’s path contract.
edgeCases: Any valid path is accepted; DFS need not return a shortest one.
Java/Python mutate the supplied maze; C++ searches a by-value copy.
An unreachable destination returns an empty path.
